cases.title: Which bombers actually received the Berlin escort?
cases.mission: The 56th Fighter Group flew two penetration sections. Near Haselünne, the 13th Combat Wing, including the 100th Bombardment Group, met the first German concentration before substantial escort cover reached it.
cases.effect: 100th Group gunner Van Pinner described the attack from his bomber. German pilot Wolfgang Kretschmer of JG 1 recalled being wounded and bailing out after a P-47 intervened. Price places the 56th Group's engagement in the same encounter.
cases.limit: The fighter return counts support along the route. It gives no continuous escort strength beside each combat wing. The accounts document an intervention but cannot count bombers saved.

cases.title: What reached Berlin after the fighter battles?
cases.mission: Target support included the 4th and 357th Fighter Groups in P-51s and the 55th in P-38s. Most supporting groups flew other legs.
cases.effect: The 1st Bomb Division missed its obscured Erkner factory objective and crews bombed the clearer Köpenick and Weissensee districts. The German Naval Staff diary independently reported bombs across Berlin between 13:10 and 13:40.
cases.limit: The city-level diary confirms that bombs reached Berlin. It cannot identify which escort group protected the bombers that dropped them or measure damage to the intended target.

cases.title: What could No. 6 Group crews see over Nuremberg?
cases.mission: Nine RCAF squadrons supplied 25 Lancasters and 93 Halifaxes. The return identifies individual aircraft and their crews as well as the dispatch total.
cases.effect: No. 408 Squadron's Flying Officer Harvey reported jettisoning after seeing no markers. Independently, Australian crewmen of No. 467 Squadron recalled seeing aircraft burning on the route.
cases.limit: The Australian evidence describes another squadron on the same operation. Visibility for one crew, losses seen en route and the raid-wide loss total have different denominators.

cases.title: A late-war group saw escorts and flak over Berlin
cases.mission: The 306th Bombardment Group recorded P-51s escorting aircraft 802-F when it had to leave formation. Its crews reported flak over Berlin, three aircraft missing and no enemy fighters seen.
cases.effect: The lead bombardier reported hits near the marshalling yard. Smoke obscured precise impacts in the group's photographs. German archival photographs document destruction at Hausvogteiplatz and at Moritzplatz after the raid.
cases.limit: The photographs locate damage on the ground. They cannot assign it to the 306th. This group's lack of observed fighters establishes no city-wide absence of German aircraft.

Allied.effort: The 6 March fighter table gives aircraft by group and escort stage. The Canadian return lists dispatches by aircraft type on 30/31 March.
Allied.losses: The Berlin fighter table reports eleven US fighters lost and identifies the groups. Nuremberg crew reports use a separate RAF night-raid population.
Allied.effect: The 100th Bombardment Group and 56th Fighter Group supply a local encounter. Night crews reported what they could see and whether they released or jettisoned.

Axis.effort: German operational maps and participant testimony identify the first and second Berlin concentrations. They leave other response stages outside these counts.
Axis.losses: Kretschmer of JG 1 describes his own bailout. His testimony cannot establish losses for the wing or reconcile Allied claims.
Axis.effect: The March 1944 naval diary records bombs falling across Berlin. In February 1945 German archive photographs document damage at specific streets and a station. Neither record attributes it to one escort or bomber group.

cases.title: Two bomber routes imposed different demands on the defenders
cases.mission: Nine groups of the 1st Bombardment Wing were dispatched toward Schweinfurt and seven of the 4th toward Regensburg. The 303rd assigned 30 crews. One aircraft failed to take off, which reconciles that figure with the 29 in the headquarters dispatch column.
cases.effect: The command reported 36 B-17s missing from 230 dispatched on the Schweinfurt operation and 24 from 146 on the Regensburg operation. The surviving reports therefore support two separate force and loss accounts.
cases.limit: The combined 60 missing aircraft cannot be apportioned to particular German groups from this return. The reported 18 US P-47 and 16 RAF Spitfire squadrons supported the wider operation.

cases.title: A bomber lost from the Regensburg force reached Switzerland
cases.mission: Fighters of II./NJG 1 engaged B-17s on the Regensburg route. Boiten identifies the 100th Group's aircraft High Life among those damaged. Its 351st Squadron casualty record names Donald Oakes as pilot.
cases.effect: Oakes described engine damage after bomb release and a wheels-up landing at Dübendorf. His crew was interned. An aircraft missing to its command could have a surviving crew and a documented landing elsewhere.
cases.limit: The US account corroborates enemy fighter damage and the outcome. It does not identify the individual German crew responsible for each hit.

cases.title: How far did damage to the bearing works travel?
cases.mission: The 303rd Bombardment Group assigned crews to VKF works No. 1. Its mission report identifies an intended factory within the wider Schweinfurt force's operation.
cases.effect: The postwar survey found that September bearing output at Schweinfurt was 35 percent of the pre-raid level. German industrial records examined for the RAF history show damage to 2.5 percent of machinery and 2.3 percent of finished stocks in the August raid.
cases.limit: Local output, damaged machinery and ready stock each use a different denominator. The survey could establish no measurable impact on essential German war production as a whole. It identifies stocks, substitutions and recovery measures.

cases.title: What did the October escort and diversion reports establish?
cases.mission: The 353rd and 56th Fighter Groups escorted the two B-17 task forces. The 352nd rendezvoused with the 93rd and 392nd Bombardment Groups' B-24s. Weather broke up B-24 assembly and only 21 of the 29 dispatched flew the subsequent diversion toward the Frisian Islands.
cases.effect: 303rd crews reported P-47s turning back for fuel. The Werneck school diary independently records German fighters and flak during the approach from the west. Schweinfurt's local raid history lists hits on the bearing works, a malt factory and Oberndorf.
cases.limit: The headquarters account says the planned withdrawal escort could not take off. The B-24 diversion belongs outside the main B-17 count. The German observers do not identify which American group they saw.

cases.title: Why are there two German defensive effort totals?
cases.mission: Jagddivisionen 1 through 5 supplied fighters against the American operation. Schmid reproduced the differing contemporary corps and command returns.
cases.effect: The I. Jagdkorps diary recorded 567 aircraft committed. The wider Luftwaffenbefehlshaber Mitte return gave 833 and included the 7. Jagddivision. Schmid lists another 49 from Luftflotte 3.
cases.limit: Command boundaries differ and neither series provides a unique-aircraft roster over Schweinfurt. Divisional participation cannot attribute American losses to a Geschwader or Gruppe.

cases.title: How much of the bearing industry was destroyed?
cases.mission: The 303rd Bombardment Group again flew against Schweinfurt. The command used reconnaissance photographs to estimate that the raid had destroyed 75 percent of local bearing production capacity.
cases.effect: The RAF history's subsequent comparison with German records gives about 20 percent of finished stocks and 3.5 percent of machinery damaged in the October operation. These figures measure different things from the wartime estimate.
cases.limit: The estimates do not identify damage attributable to the 303rd. A factory's damaged machinery, stock on hand, later output and national war production must each be measured separately.

Allied.effort: The August plan names four P-47 groups. The October result names separate groups covering the two B-17 task forces and the B-24 rendezvous. Of 29 B-24s dispatched, only 21 flew the diversion.
Allied.losses: August losses split by route and group. Of 60 B-17s lost in October the headquarters account classed two as flak, eighteen as enemy aircraft and forty as cause unknown.
Allied.effect: Group records identify assigned works and early returns. The command's October estimate of industrial destruction can be checked against records from the factories.

Axis.effort: Five named night-fighter wings contributed elements in daylight in August. Two NJG 1 Gruppen can be followed by sortie. In October, five fighter divisions and competing command return totals are identified.
Axis.losses: Boiten records the return of damaged II./NJG 1 aircraft at St. Trond on 17 August. Contemporary confirmation decisions qualify the initial German claims. A loss roster for the entire October response remains open.
Axis.effect: The postwar industrial survey distinguishes September Schweinfurt output from the effect on German war production. The RAF history separates stock loss from machine damage.

cases.title: What did the Canadian night force contribute at Leipzig?
cases.mission: No. 6 Group supplied 31 Lancasters from two squadrons and 98 Halifaxes from ten squadrons to the opening night raid. No. 419 Squadron's Form 541 records its own crews' work.
cases.effect: The group reconstruction identifies eighteen crews that failed to return, totalling 128 missing crew members. The original 419 diary allows individual sorties to be checked inside this national group.
cases.limit: The missing count describes the first reporting outcome. The Canadian group's 129 aircraft exclude other Bomber Command groups. This night operation preceded the Eighth Air Force's daylight attack.

cases.title: Which German divisions met the daylight offensive?
cases.mission: The German account places 1. and 2. Jagddivision against the northern force and 2. and 3. Jagddivision against the main force. The 2. Jagddivision appears in both contexts.
cases.effect: The German account separates 362 fighters employed from 155 that actually entered combat. A commitment total would overstate the number reported to have fought.
cases.limit: Wood's wider German unit table also lists Gruppen from the fourth, fifth and seventh divisions and Ostmark. Its entries measure claims and losses by unit. They cannot supply a divisional split of the 155 aircraft reported in combat by the corps.

cases.title: Can the German claimant for one missing American escort be identified?
cases.mission: John Mattie of the 353rd Fighter Squadron, 354th Fighter Group, lost P-51 43-12161 during the escort operation and became a prisoner. Missing Air Crew Report 2329 and his diary survive.
cases.effect: Heinz Bär of 6./JG 1 received official German credit for a P-51 in the area. A comparison of the two pilots' records favours Bär, with another claim by Hans-Heinrich König of 3./JG 11 still unresolved.
cases.limit: The records establish Mattie's fate and Bär's claim independently. The authors identify the connection as probable. The claim record lacks a matching American serial.

cases.title: Steyr and Fiume had different bomber and escort histories
cases.mission: The 2nd, 97th and 301st Bombardment Groups struck Steyr with 87 B-17s. Weather separated the 99th, whose 27 attacked Fiume. The 5th Wing reported that attacks on the Steyr bombers continued until the four withdrawal fighter groups appeared south of the target.
cases.effect: The wing recorded 16 B-17s lost in the Steyr operation, ten from the 2nd Group. The municipal account for Steyr records 212 dead, 371 injured and over 1,000 homeless. It describes the destruction of Building M, light damage to the engine factory and an intact heat-treatment section.
cases.limit: The Steyr account cannot attribute individual impacts to a bomber group. The German I. Jagdkorps figure of 336 on 24 February covers its own reporting area and includes repeat sorties. It cannot establish the fighter force over Steyr.

cases.title: What could reconnaissance establish about Gotha?
cases.mission: The 392nd and 445th Bombardment Groups flew B-24s against the Gotha aircraft works. Hal Turell of the 445th's 703rd Squadron recalled that thirteen of the group's 25 aircraft failed to return.
cases.effect: The post-strike reconnaissance photograph shows damage to the works. The 392nd briefing's estimate of potential enemy aircraft production forgone was an expectation contingent on the duration of disruption.
cases.limit: Structural damage and American group losses are observable in different records. They cannot establish a definite number of aircraft the factory failed to deliver or which defending formation shot down each bomber.

Allied.effort: The Canadian Leipzig night roster, the 5th Wing's Steyr and Fiume assignment, two Gotha group records and four withdrawal fighter groups cover distinct operations.
Allied.losses: The Leipzig night count records missing Canadian crews. Steyr losses are separately bounded to the 5th Wing, and Gotha losses here cover the 445th Group.
Allied.effect: B-17 records distinguish Steyr from Fiume. Gotha post-strike photography documents structural damage. A briefing forecast supplies no measured production loss.

Axis.effort: The corps counted 362 fighters employed and 155 in combat on 20 February. A wider claims and casualty register identifies 27 Gruppen and their reported bases. The Austrian response on 24 February remains unresolved.
Axis.losses: Wood gives separate damage columns for German Gruppen on 20 February. III./ZG 26 alone has ten aircraft in the 60–100 percent bracket and three at lower damage. These figures cannot verify individual Allied claims.
Axis.effect: Steyr's municipal account distinguishes factory sections, casualties and housing losses. The evidence cannot disaggregate the effects of individual bomber or escort groups.
